**Dataset Description**

**Data Source**  
Source: [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yasserh/housing-prices-dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yasserh/housing-prices-dataset)  
Name: Housing Prices Dataset  
Size: 546 Rows x 13 Columns  
The purpose of the regression model was to predict house prices of certain houses in the future based on the houses’ qualities and traits, such as area, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, stories, and more.

**Target Variable**  
The target variable of the data set was price. The model was created to calculate prices based on x variables in order to predict house prices in the future.

**Key Insights**  
Important Findings:

* House prices generally increased as area increased  
* House prices decreased when houses were less furnished than if they were furnished  
* House prices have a generally linear relationship with area (positive relationship) and furnishing status (negative relationship)

**Data Preprocessing** 

**Missing Values**  
The dataset had no missing values, so nothing had to be handled.

**Outliers**  
Because the data was 2 dimensional, outlier detection while taking into account both of the variables was not possible. As a result, no action was taken to remove outliers, and all outliers were kept.

**Feature Engineering**  
To feature engineer the dataset, encoding and scaling methods were used. This helped make the regression line more accurate and predictive of the data. This helped increase the reliability of the model and better train the AI.

**Encoding & Scaling**  
First, the variables were separated into numerical and categorical x-variables. Using pandas methods, the categorical “yes/no” variables were converted into numeric variables using get\_dummies(drop\_first=True). After that, the categorical variables (now numerical) and the initial numerical variables were concatenated, to get a fully numerical list of the x-variables being used. To scale the variables, StandardScaler was used, to ensure that variables with large ranges such as area did not dominate models that rely on distance or magnitude.

**Train-Test Split**  
The split ratio used for the train-test split was 80% for training, and 20% for testing. This allowed for increased model accuracy and prediction reliability.

**Models & Results**

**Models Implemented**  
The following models were tested:

* Linear Regression  
* K-Nearest Neighbors Regression  
* Random Forest Regression  
* Support Vector Regression

**Performance Comparison**

| Model | MSE (Test) | R² | RSME (Test) | MAE (Test) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Linear Regression | 1003826757651.160 | 0.652 | 1001911.552 | 750333.971 |
| KNN | 1203760841466.349 | 0.582 | 1097160.354 | 806031.633 |
| Support Vector | 3000208447756.047 | \-0.041 | 1732110.980 | 1259213.478 |
| Random Forest | 1351630707249.537 | 0.531 | 1162596.537 | 895403.817 |

**Best Model**  
The best model was the Linear Regression Model, since it had the smallest values for mean absolute error, mean squared error, and root mean squared error. This meant that the model best captured all of the data points and had the best predicting power for future data points. 5 features that this model has are that it takes into significant account of the categorical variables, it has the highest R value, it has the smallest error values, it shows the strongest positive correlation between the x and y variables, and it is the most representative of the data.

**Findings & Conclusion**

**Key Findings**  
Because of the linear regression model, I found that there was a moderately strong linear positive correlation between the x-variables such as area, number of bathrooms, number of bedrooms, etc., and the y-variable, price. The model showed a positive correlation through its r value, which was calculated by finding the square root of the r² value as shown in the graph above. The model also represents how 65.2% of the change in price was a result of the change in the x-variables. Some surprising insights found were that the r value was strongly positive, and that the linear model was more representative of the data than the other models.

**Challenges**  
The main difficulties encountered were deciding what to do with the data outliers, since there was no efficient way to remove outliers that considered both the x and y values, rather than just 1\. Another challenge faced was creating the graphs that represented how well the linear regression model represented the data.

**Conclusion**  
By testing multiple models and assessing their error scores, the best model was determined that was the most representative of the data. This model was the linear regression model, and was the most predictive and accurate out of all of the other models. This allows for more reliable and credible predictions to be made in the future to predict house prices when certain criteria are given to the model. These criteria would be the independent variables, of which the model would take into account and then accurately predict the house’s price, using artificial intelligence and machine learning. This model can be used in practical applications in the real world to predict house prices for other houses, as well as give real estate agents more data-driven and justifiable house prices.

**Future Work**  
In the future, work could be done to remove outliers while considering both x and y variables, as well as use another model type rather than just the 4 tested here. This will allow for a more reliable and accurate model to be produced, since more models are being tested.
